brief.text:
The clearest thing in today's data is the cost of fuelling a ship. VLSFO — very low sulphur fuel oil, the main bunker fuel burned by most merchant ships — jumped in Asia and Europe this morning: Singapore is $882.50 a tonne, up $60.50 or 7.4%, Fujairah $856.50, up $34.00 (+4.1%), and Rotterdam $743.50, up $26.00 (+3.6%). Houston went the other way, down $2.00 to $737.00. For anyone fixing a voyage charter, where the owner pays for fuel, a move of that size east of Suez eats directly into earnings and will show up in the freight numbers owners quote you today.

Crude was firmer but far less dramatic: Brent $96.42 a barrel, up 0.58 (+0.6%), WTI $89.06, up 0.50 (+0.6%), with the Brent–WTI spread at $7.36. Gasoil rose 1.2% to $4.31 a gallon and gasoline 1.0% to $2.65, while US Henry Hub gas fell 3.6% to $3.12. The diesel crack — refining margin over Brent — stands at $84.50. The data does not show why Singapore and Fujairah bunkers rose so much more than crude or than Houston; one possible factor is the headline that a tanker was confirmed struck in the Gulf with Iran claiming a VLCC (very large crude carrier) sinking, but the data does not confirm that link. No freight index refreshed today: the Baltic Dry Index was 2,980 points on Friday 13 November, Capesize 4,719, Panamax 2,118, Supramax 1,836, and the tanker TCE figures — time charter equivalent, a voyage's earnings expressed as dollars per day — were last seen on Sunday 15 November, with VLCC TD3C at $1,078,714/day and Suezmax TD20 at $151,300/day.

Running stories moved. The Black Sea escalated: three commercial vessels were struck by drones off Romania's Sulina anchorage, prompting Romanian fighter jets to scramble, and an abandoned freighter hit two months ago is drifting toward Bulgarian waters. Hormuz also developed, with the confirmed Gulf tanker strike and Iran's mine claims. The Jones Act waiver, shadow-fleet sanctions, Russian diesel export curbs and the suspended US port fees on Chinese-built ships had no news today and are unchanged.

Watch two things. First, whether the Baltic tanker and dry indices refresh tomorrow — they are your only read on whether today's bunker spike is being passed into rates. Second, further Black Sea strikes, which bear on grain and dry bulk loadings and on war-risk insurance for the region.

storylines.title: Attacks and blockade enforcement around Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have continued into November. Today's trade press reports a tanker confirmed struck in the Gulf, with Iran claiming two tankers hit mines and a VLCC sunk.
storylines.why_it_matters: Hull strikes and crew-safety concerns raise war-risk premiums for Arabian Gulf liftings and shrink the pool of willing owners; depressed transit volumes reshape crude and product ton-miles.
storylines.latest: A tanker was confirmed struck in the Gulf and Iran claims a VLCC sinking and two tankers hit by mines. Separately, Fujairah VLSFO rose $34.00 (+4.1%) to $856.50/t today, though the data does not establish a link.

storylines.title: US Jones Act waiver extended again
storylines.what: President Trump is extending the waiver allowing energy companies and traders to move oil, fertilizer and other commodities between US ports on foreign-flagged ships for another 90 days. The pause has now stretched past 230 days.
storylines.why_it_matters: The waiver keeps foreign-flag tonnage eligible for US coastwise cargoes, affecting demand for US-flag ships and the employment of product tankers in domestic trades.

storylines.title: Sanctions and evasion in the shadow fleet
storylines.what: US sanctions have expanded across Cuban maritime entities and Iranian false-flag registry networks, while the dark fleet is described as a parallel fleet that has tripled since 2022. The US Treasury may now allow companies to buy sanctioned vessels and return them to legitimate trade case by case.
storylines.why_it_matters: Registry fraud and designations force charterers and insurers to re-verify documents and positions; a licensing route back to legitimate trade could return tonnage to the compliant fleet.

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia arrangement on extra diesel for the US market has met political opposition, while Russia has extended a ban on most diesel exports to end-January.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment.

storylines.title: US port fees on Chinese-built and Chinese-operated ships
storylines.what: The US administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months while trade talks continue.
storylines.why_it_matters: The fees, if reinstated, would change the cost of deploying Chinese-built tonnage into US trades and affect chartering preferences across sectors.

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia arrangement on extra diesel for the US market has met political opposition, while Russia has extended a ban on most diesel exports to end-January.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment.

storylines.title: US port fees on Chinese-built and Chinese-operated ships
storylines.what: The US administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months while trade talks continue.
storylines.why_it_matters: The fees, if reinstated, would change the cost of deploying Chinese-built tonnage into US trades and affect chartering preferences across sectors.
